content: 1. This indicator evaluates the availability of viral load (VL) testing in a country and ensures the proper interpretation of VL testing data. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends routine VL testing at 6 months and 12 months after antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation, and annually thereafter. 3. Many countries are still in the process of expanding their VL testing capacity. 4. This indicator is essential to determine whether VL suppression data from routine testing is representative of all patients on ART. 5. The numerator is the number of ART patients with at least one routine VL test result during the reporting period. 6. The denominator is the number of ART patients who have been on ART for at least 6 months. 7. Measurement involves program records, such as ART registers, cohort reporting forms, and patient records. It is critical to avoid duplicate records and double-counting when identifying the numerator. 8. The denominator excludes patients who have died, transferred to another clinic, or are classified as lost to follow-up. 9. Disaggregation is done by gender (male, female, transgender), age groups (e.g., 0–4, 5–9, 10–14, etc.), key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, people in prisons, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals), and other priority populations. 10. Early VL testing at 6 months measures progress in promoting early adherence and VL suppression (VLS) on ART. 11. WHO recommends VL testing at 6 months after ART initiation to assess VLS and identify individuals needing intensive adherence counseling and follow-up in cases of non-suppression. 12. This indicator is critical for understanding early non-adherence risks and enabling interventions to improve adherence, VLS, and reduce the risk of HIV drug resistance. 13. The numerator is the number of ART patients eligible for VL monitoring at 6 months after ART initiation who had VL monitoring and received their results. 14. The denominator is the number of ART patients eligible for VL monitoring at 6 months after ART initiation during the reporting period. 15. Measurement involves program records, such as ART registers, cohort reporting forms, patient records, and laboratory information systems. 16. The time window for early VL monitoring includes a margin of ±1 month, meaning the test can occur between 5 and 7 months after ART initiation. 17. Disaggregation is done by gender, age, key populations, and other priority populations. 18. The percentage of people receiving ART with VL ≥1000 copies/mL who received a follow-up VL test within 6 months after enhanced adherence counseling measures the extent to which individuals with non-suppressed VL receive appropriate follow-up testing. 19. Virologic suppression is essential to achieving the 95–95–95 goals, including HIV elimination. 20. The numerator is the number of people on ART with VL ≥1000 copies/mL who received a follow-up VL test within 6 months after the initial test. 21. The denominator is the number of people on ART with VL ≥1000 copies/mL during the reporting period. 22. Measurement involves program records, such as ART registers and electronic medical records (EMRs). 23. The recommended maximum reporting period is 12 months, with shorter intervals (e.g., 3 months) recommended where feasible. 24. Disaggregation is done by gender, age, key populations, ART regimen, and receipt of enhanced adherence counseling. 25. The percentage of ART patients with treatment-limiting toxicity measures the incidence of serious antiretroviral (ARV) toxicities among ART patients. 26. As ARV use scales up, individuals living with HIV may experience prolonged exposure to ARVs and potential ARV-related toxicities. 27. ARV-related toxicities are common reasons for ART non-adherence, treatment discontinuation, or drug substitution. 28. Information on toxicity prevalence informs national guidelines and efforts to prevent and limit drug toxicity. 29. The numerator is the number of ART patients who stopped treatment or switched regimens due to toxicity during the reporting period. 30. The denominator is the number of ART patients during the reporting period. 31. Measurement involves program records, such as ART registers, cohort reporting forms, and patient records. 32. Treatment-limiting toxicity is defined as a serious adverse drug reaction resulting in drug discontinuation or substitution. 33. Disaggregation is done by gender, age, key populations, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. 34. The percentage of eligible people living with HIV on ART who initiated tuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment (TPT) measures the extent to which ART patients started treatment for latent TB infection. 35. TPT is critical for preventing TB-related morbidity and mortality among people living with HIV. 36. Recent guidelines have expanded eligibility criteria for TPT among people living with HIV. 37. This indicator tracks progress in scaling up TPT coverage in light of recent global commitments and targets. 38. The numerator is the number of ART patients who initiated TPT during the reporting period. 39. The denominator is the number of ART patients eligible for TPT during the reporting period. 40. Measurement involves program records, such as ART registers. 41. Disaggregation is done by gender, age, type of TPT regimen, and ART initiation status. 42. The percentage of people living with HIV on ART who completed a course of TPT measures the effectiveness of scaled-up TPT programs by assessing the proportion of patients who completed the recommended course. 43. Many countries have made progress in initiating TPT among eligible individuals, but completion rates remain poor or unknown. 44. Assessing TPT completion is a critical element of the TB/HIV service cascade. 45. The numerator is the number of ART patients who completed a course of TPT during the reporting period. 46. The denominator is the number of ART patients who initiated any course of TPT during the previous reporting period. 47. Measurement involves program records, such as ART registers. 48. Disaggregation is done by gender, age, type of TPT regimen, and ART initiation status. 49. The percentage of people living with HIV with TB symptoms who receive a rapid molecular test as a first diagnostic test measures the proportion of individuals screened positive for TB symptoms who receive a recommended diagnostic test. 50. People living with HIV should be screened for TB symptoms and, if positive, tested for TB. 51. WHO recommends rapid molecular diagnostic tests, such as Xpert MTB/RIF, as the first test for TB diagnosis among people living with HIV. 52. The numerator is the number of people living with HIV and TB symptoms who were tested using a rapid molecular test as a first test during the reporting period. 53. The denominator is the number of people living with HIV screened for TB and found to have symptoms during the reporting period. 54. Measurement involves program records, such as laboratory registers and ART registers. 55. Disaggregation is done by gender, age, key populations, and pregnant or breastfeeding women. 56. The percentage of HIV-positive pregnant women who are virally suppressed at labor and delivery measures VL suppression at the time of delivery among HIV-positive pregnant women. 57. VL suppression at delivery is a critical service quality measure during the vertical transmission risk period. 58. Two denominators are used: one based on program data (women on ART delivering in a facility with a VL test) and one based on population data (all women delivering in a facility regardless of ART status). 59. The numerator is the number of HIV-positive pregnant women on ART during pregnancy and delivery who were virally suppressed (VL <1000 copies/mL) at delivery. 60. The denominator is the number of HIV-positive pregnant women on ART during pregnancy who delivered at a facility and had a VL test during delivery. 61. Measurement involves program records, such as PMTCT registers. 62. Disaggregation is done by age and timing of ART initiation. 63. The percentage of HIV-exposed infants who receive a virological test for HIV within 2 months (and 12 months) of birth measures early HIV diagnosis in infants. 64. High coverage of early virological testing enables early ART initiation in children with confirmed HIV infection.
